syllabus.clause: buffered I/O goes through the page cache (writeback, readahead, dirty-page throttling). Direct I/O (O_DIRECT) bypasses it under alignment and completion constraints (logical block size, aligned buffers). posix_fadvise.

items.item: DONTNEED's own documented non-binding status is exactly why this topic measures its effect directly rather than trusting the documentation alone; a hint that the kernel is free to ignore could, in principle, do nothing in a given kernel version or configuration, which only an executed measurement can rule out.

items.item: The buffered-versus-direct comparison uses two separate files rather than reopening one file both ways, specifically so an earlier buffered read's own cache effect cannot leak into the O_DIRECT measurement through shared page-cache state for that inode.

items.item: O_DIRECT leaving zero resident pages is not merely the absence of a speed-up; it is direct evidence that the read path taken by O_DIRECT genuinely does not pass through the same kernel structure a buffered read populates, which is a stronger and more specific claim than 'O_DIRECT is slower.'

at.step: Measured: the buffered read left every single page resident in the cache, and the exact same read through O_DIRECT left none resident at all

items.item: The dirty-page explanation for DONTNEED's apparent failure right after a write is not a guess; it follows directly from the same man page's own documented caveat quoted in this topic, and the executed example demonstrates the contrapositive directly: fsyncing first makes the very same DONTNEED call succeed.

items.item: This topic deliberately defers any claim about durability to topic 40, even though fsync appears in its own example code as a baseline-clearing helper; using fsync to produce a clean measurement is not the same claim as fsync making data durable, and conflating the two here would pre-empt topic 40's own real subject.

at.step: The man page is explicit: any unwritten, dirty page will not be freed by DONTNEED at all — fsync or fdatasync has to write it back first, or the hint has nothing clean to discard

items.item: This topic's three measured behaviors are not three unrelated facts about three different syscalls; each one is a different point of control over the exact same underlying kernel data structure, the page cache for one file's pages, which is why the lesson step frames them as one shared resource rather than three separate topics.

at.step: Readahead, DONTNEED, and O_DIRECT are the same page cache, pulled three different directions: bring pages in early, push them back out on request, or never let them in to begin with
